readerTitle: Your first price is the one you'll be stuck with
caseNote: 가상 사례 (정리 수납 서비스 두 곳, 레스토랑 대상 회계 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 첫 거래 가격에 관해 1차 출처로 확인할 수 있는 기업 사례가 마땅치 않아, company_story 대신 two_businesses 형식으로 바꿨습니다.
insight: 첫 거래 가격은 매출보다 정보와 기준점이다. 할인을 주더라도 정가를 먼저 밝히고, 무언가를 받고, 끝나는 날을 정한다.
misconception: 처음에는 일단 싸게 받아 고객을 모으고, 나중에 가격을 올리면 된다.

sources.text: 영업·가격 책정의 일반 원칙 (기준점 효과, 할인과 교환 조건)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 정가 $60의 30% 할인 = $60 × 0.7 = $42. 시간당 $25에서 $60으로 올리면 인상률 (60 − 25) ÷ 25 = 140%.

cards.title: Your first price is the one you'll be stuck with
body: Two professional organizers start out in the same city in the same month. Same skills, same reviews, same hustle.
Six months later, one is fully booked and barely paying her bills. The other has fewer clients and a healthy business. The difference started with the first price each of them said out loud.

image.label: Two organizers with very different price tags on their calendars
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 거리에 나란히 선 두 정리 수납 전문가. 왼쪽은 꽉 찬 달력 옆에 작은 "$25/hr" 가격표와 빈 지갑, 오른쪽은 듬성듬성한 달력 옆에 "$60/hr" 가격표와 넉넉한 지갑. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your very first client asks your price.
body: You've just launched a home organizing service. You believe the work is worth about $60 an hour, the going rate nearby. You have no reviews yet, and a first client is on the phone.

options.text: $25 an hour, to get in the door and earn reviews
options.feedback: You'll likely win the job. But the client now thinks your work is worth $25, and so will everyone they refer.

options.text: $60 an hour, with 30% off for first clients who give a review and photos
options.feedback: You still offer a deal, but the real price is on the table and the discount buys you something. You give up some cash now to protect every price later.

options.text: Free for the first three clients, then full price
options.feedback: Free work brings photos fast. But a yes to free tells you nothing about whether anyone will pay, and the jump to $60 will feel steep.

cards.title: Six months later.
body: Maya quoted $25. Jonah quoted $60 and gave early clients 30% off, with the full price printed on every invoice. To reach $60, Maya now needs a **140% price rise**. Jonah's clients already expect it.

breakdown.label: Jonah's first price
breakdown.detail: $60 list, 30% off, shown on the invoice

breakdown.label: Jonah's price now
breakdown.detail: The discount simply ended on schedule

cards.title: Your first price is an anchor and a test
body: When you price your first deals, you are doing two things. You set an **anchor**: the number customers and their friends will remember as "what this costs." And you run a test: does anyone value this enough to pay a real price?
A very low price wins the deal but fails both jobs. It anchors low, and a yes at $25 can't tell you whether people would pay $60.

cards.title: Three rules for first deals.
body: If you discount early, make the discount do work for you.
list: **Say the real price first.** Then show the discount against it, in writing.
**Trade, don't give.** Ask for a review, photos, a referral or a longer commitment in return.
**Set an end date.** "For my first five clients" or "for three months" makes the full price the default.
cards.callout: A discount with a reason and an end date doesn't move your anchor.
cards.softwareNote: Early software customers often get a founding discount. Showing list price on the contract and tying the discount to a case study or annual prepay keeps renewals from becoming a fight.

cards.title: Low prices attract the wrong signal.
body: Maya's calendar filled up, which felt like proof. But many of her clients chose her *because* she was cheap. When she raised prices, they left for someone cheaper.

Jonah heard more no's early on. Each one taught him something: the pitch was unclear, or the client wasn't the right fit. The clients who said yes at $60 were the ones who valued the work, and they referred people like themselves.

cards.title: Sometimes a low first price is right.
body: If you genuinely don't know whether your service works, a reduced price can be fair. The customer is taking a risk on you. Just name that trade openly, so it isn't mistaken for your real price.

The opposite mistake exists too. A price far above what your first results can justify kills deals before you learn anything. Aim for the price you expect to charge once you can deliver well, not a fantasy number.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You run a new bookkeeping service for restaurants. Your standard fee is $1,500 a month. A group with four restaurants wants to sign, but asks for 50% off for the first year because you're new.

options.text: Accept 50% off for a year. Four restaurants is a great logo
options.feedback: You'd win a strong reference, but give up $9,000 and teach them $750 is the real price. Renewal becomes a 100% price rise.

options.text: List price on the contract, 20% off for three months in exchange for a case study and two referrals
options.feedback: You still give a real deal and get proof and introductions in return. The full price takes over on a date both sides agreed to.

options.text: Refuse any discount. Full price or nothing
options.feedback: It protects your anchor, but you may lose a valuable first client over a small, time-limited concession you could have traded for something useful.

cards.title: Quote the real price, then decide what a discount should buy.
body: Early prices stick. Show your list price, trade any discount for something you need, and give it an end date.
**Try it today:** write down your real price. Then list three things a first customer could give you in exchange for a discount.
